pageProps.body:
🖼️ Culture Under Control|文化審查

Related: 🎬 Films & Documentaries | 📕 Book Censorship under the NSL | 📰 Press Freedom under Siege | 🕯️ Tiananmen Vigil

Hong Kong built M+ and the West Kowloon Cultural District to crown itself as Asia's world city of art — a US$3-billion museum of visual culture meant to stand beside Tate Modern and the Pompidou. It opened in November 2021, eighteen months into the National Security Law. Since then the censorship that closed the city's newsrooms and emptied its library shelves has reached its galleries and cinemas too — rarely by public ban, more often by a quiet edit: a work withdrawn before anyone can ask to see it, a title changed to satisfy a censor, a screening cancelled for "technical reasons." This page gathers those cases as they surface, and keeps the institutions' own notices before they can be edited away.

M+ cancels Hou Hsiao-hsien's The Time to Live and the Time to Die (Nov 2026)

Watch: active — this story is developing.

On 13 November 2026, with no advance warning, M+ posted a notice on its website cancelling both scheduled screenings of 《童年往事》 The Time to Live and the Time to Die (1985) — the semi-autobiographical masterpiece by Taiwanese director Hou Hsiao-hsien (侯孝賢), photographed by Mark Lee Ping-bing (李屏賓). The notice, in English only, reads in full:

"Due to technical reasons, all the screenings of The Time to Live and the Time to Die have been cancelled. Ticket holders are entitled to a full refund and will be contacted with details."

The two screenings — 22 Nov 2026, 14:30 and 12 Dec 2026, 14:00 — are both now marked Cancelled on the film's page. No further explanation of the "technical reasons" has been given.

What makes the stated reason hard to credit:

  • Only this one film was cut. It was the opening title of "Lightcatcher: The Cinematography of Mark Lee Ping-Bing" (追光逐影：李屏賓的攝影藝術), a ten-film programme running 21 Nov – 26 Dec 2026. The other nine screenings are untouched — including two other Hou Hsiao-hsien films shot by the same cinematographer, The Assassin (刺客聶隱娘) and Flowers of Shanghai (海上花), and his Café Lumière (珈琲時光) in a separate strand. A "technical" fault that strikes one 137-minute print in a retrospective and no other is an unusual kind of fault.
  • The Time to Live and the Time to Die is a canonical work of Taiwan New Cinema with no protest or security content — a childhood memoir of a mainland-émigré family in 1950s–60s southern Taiwan. The sensitivity, if any, lies not in the film but in what it stands for: a landmark of Taiwanese cinema, screened as cross-strait cultural exchange narrows.
  • At the time of capture the museum's own two pages disagreed: the film page showed both screenings cancelled, while the programme page still listed the 22 Nov screening with no cancelled marker — suggesting a hurried, unannounced change.

Preserved evidence (captured 13 Nov 2026, before the notice can be edited):

  • Film page with the cancellation notice — screenshot · HTML cold copy · live page
  • Programme page (still showing the screening) — screenshot · HTML cold copy · live page

Open questions being tracked: does M+ give any real explanation of the "technical reasons"? Is the film quietly reinstated or permanently dropped? Do other outlets (HKFP, SCMP, The Witness) confirm it, and is it part of a wider pattern of cancellations? Updates are added here as they surface.

Earlier cases

M+ renames a banned Zhang Yuan film to screen it (2024)

To show the Chinese independent film 《北京雜種》 Beijing Bastards (1993) by Zhang Yuan, M+ screened it under the neutral title "A Film by Zhang Yuan," a change made to obtain a licence from Hong Kong's film censors shortly before the public screening. The retitling — stripping a work of the name its own maker gave it in order to let an audience see it at all — became a widely-cited example of how the museum navigates the censorship regime. (SCMP · Artnet)

M+ opens without Ai Weiwei's Tiananmen photograph (2021)

As M+ prepared to open in 2021, pro-Beijing politicians claimed that Ai Weiwei's photograph "Study of Perspective: Tiananmen Square" — the artist raising his middle finger at the square — could breach the National Security Law. The museum, which had earlier said showing such works would be "no problem," announced it had no plans to display the work, and removed its image from the museum's online collection hub. The institution opened in November 2021 under open accusations of self-censorship. (AP via Smithsonian · Fortune · SCMP: Storm over M+)

Why it matters

A museum is supposed to be where a society keeps what it has decided is worth remembering. When the keeping becomes selective — when a film can be cancelled without a reason, a work withheld before it is ever hung, a title altered to pass a censor — the record itself is quietly rewritten. The cases here are small next to a jailed publisher or a banned song, which is precisely why they are easy to miss and worth preserving: they mark the point at which control stops needing to announce itself.

Preserve the record

If you hold programmes, tickets, booking-page screenshots, email notices to ticket-holders, or press coverage of a cancelled, altered or withdrawn exhibition, screening or performance at M+, the West Kowloon Cultural District, the Hong Kong Palace Museum, LCSD venues or any Hong Kong cultural institution — especially the institution's own notice before it is edited — please help add it: see Participation. A cancellation is easy to erase from a website; a captured notice is not.

noteIndex.title: SHKO(Save Hong Kong Online)
noteIndex.body:
[![Great Extinction](/assets/extinctions.jpeg)](/notes/wx39zljncctue32jn06u29u/) 
> (_Courtesy: [Hong Kong Freepress](https://hongkongfp.com/2021/11/28/explainer-over-50-groups-gone-in-11-months-how-hong-kongs-pro-democracy-forces-crumbled/), 2021_) 

SHKO (Save Hong Kong Online) is a community-driven project dedicated to preserving the rapidly disappearing websites and online resources of Hong Kong’s civil society and independent media since 2019. In response to the sweeping shutdowns caused by political changes in Hong Kong, we aim to safeguard digital heritage before it vanishes. This project is anonymous, open source, and supported by a global network of contributors.

While most sites in our archive were forced offline due to Hong Kong’s political deterioration, it’s important to note that [[RFA Cantonese|sites.rfa_cantonese]] is the only site here closed not because of Hong Kong’s situation, but due to internal political decisions in the United States.

Explore our full list of preserved sites and archives on the [Collections page](/notes/wx39zljncctue32jn06u29u/).

Recent work: documenting the [[Hong Kong Fire 2025|hong-kong-fire-2025]] tragedy at Wang Fuk Court (168 dead, ongoing probes into flammable mesh/foam, bid-rigging, and a judge-led review), including activism, timeline, and investigation subpages; and the [[⚖️ Jimmy Lai case|faces-of-the-crackdown.jimmy-lai]] — Apple Daily founder sentenced to 20 years under the National Security Law (Feb 2026), with coverage of press freedom impact and international response; and [[🎵 Glory to Hong Kong|glory-to-hong-kong]] — the 2019 protest anthem and the 2024 court order that made it the first song banned in Hong Kong since the 1997 handover; and [[📕 Book Censorship under the NSL|book-censorship]] — how Hong Kong criminalised the printed word, from the banned Sheep Village children's-book trilogy (whose speech-therapist authors were jailed for sedition) and purged public libraries to the 2026 bookshop raids; and [[🗽 Statues & Monuments|statues]] — how Hong Kong's public monuments to Tiananmen and the 2019 protests (the Pillar of Shame, the Goddess of Democracy, Lady Liberty) were removed, seized as police evidence, and driven into exile abroad; and [[⚖️ The Hong Kong 47|hong-kong-47]] — the largest National Security Law case, in which 45 pro-democracy figures were jailed for up to 10 years over a 2020 opposition primary election; and [[🕯️ Tiananmen Vigil|tiananmen-vigil]] — the thirty-year Victoria Park candlelight vigil for the 1989 crackdown, the largest June 4th commemoration on Chinese soil, now banned and its organisers jailed; and [[✊ Faces of the Crackdown|faces-of-the-crackdown]] — a human index to the publishers, students, unionists and clergy jailed, exiled or tried under the National Security Law; and [[🎬 Films & Documentaries|films]] — the protest movement on film, a decade of documentaries and features (Ten Years, Revolution of Our Times, the Joshua Wong doc) now largely banned or unshowable in Hong Kong, gathered with their trailers; and [[📰 Press Freedom under Siege|press-freedom]] — how one of Asia's freest presses was dismantled in five years, from the raids that closed Apple Daily and Stand News to the revived sedition law now reaching lone online reporters; and [[🗣️ Cantonese Under Pressure|cantonese]] — how Hong Kong's mother tongue, spoken by nearly everyone yet official to no one, is squeezed in schools and officialdom, from the Education Bureau's 2014 "not an official language" gaffe to a prestigious school's 2026 attempt to forbid Cantonese in a graduation video; and [[🖼️ Culture Under Control|culture-under-control]] — how Hong Kong's flagship cultural institutions, above all the M+ museum, quietly police their own programmes under the National Security Law, from Ai Weiwei's withheld Tiananmen photograph at the 2021 opening to the 2026 cancellation of a Hou Hsiao-hsien classic for unexplained "technical reasons."

## Goals
- To preserve as much information as possible before its disappearance during Hong Kong's great transition
- To illustrate a viable method that everyone can use to help preserve online heritage with no pains
- To demonstrate global collaborations to save local digital heritages with best practices

## Quick Facts

We are working on over dozens of [[websites or online causes | sites]] in Hong Kong in the past two decades which has been forced to shutdown or at the brink of disappearing. We'd welcome anyone help [[contribute | participation]] to the content and/or [[sponsor | sponsorship]] our program to sustain it together. 

Examples:
- [[sites.appledaily]] (Extincted)
- [[sites.inmediahk]] (In Danger)
